extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent examiners, Federal Circuit judges, and pro se appellants involved in §101/§102 disputes
extracted.subtask_description: A Federal Circuit petition for rehearing (including en banc rehearing) challenging the panel's §101 eligibility and §102 anticipation analyses, asserting legal and procedural errors and reliance on precedent. It focuses on whether claimed lipid compositions (dosage, casings, intermixtures, ratios) are products of nature or patentable subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter — non-natural composition limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim limitations such as “dosage of omega-6 and omega-3”, “casings providing controlled delivery”, and “intermixtures [of lipids] in defined ratios” are not products of nature and render the claimed compositions structurally distinct on their face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page argues these limitations impart functional structure and materially change properties of lipids versus natural counterparts (e.g., oils/nuts/seeds). Cites Myriad and Chakrabarty as controlling precedent that products of nature are ineligible but structural/functional alterations can make compositions patentable. Examples: Claim 65 (dosage + casings + intermixture) and Claims 102, 107, 109, 128 asserted to be structurally distinct. The petition faults the panel for accepting that the claims are products of nature despite acknowledging these limitations elsewhere (Op10–12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner burden — show natural counterpart exists
rubrics_metrics.description: The Examiner must provide evidence that a natural counterpart exists for the claimed composition; an admission that no natural counterpart appears to exist weighs against a product-of-nature finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellant cites Examiner admission: 'Relative to the compositions of Claims 102, 107, and 119, there does not appear to be a naturally occurring counterpart to all of these elements present together in the claimed combination' (Appx7776). The petition contends the panel overlooked that admission when affirming ineligibility under §101. Use prosecution record and examiner statements to check burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermixture as structural limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'intermixture' can be construed as a structural limitation; product claims comprising intermixtures are patentable when the structure is unknown, complex, or expected to have distinct properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Garnero and Abbott: intermixture is capable of construction as structural. The petition argues that mixtures of lipids from different sources necessarily change physical/chemical properties and thus are not mere natural products. Where structure is complex or not fully known, courts should treat 'intermixture' as structural rather than disregarding it under §101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed matter/functional instructions combined with product may be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that combines printed matter (instructions/serving) with a product is patentable if the printed matter has a functional relationship to the product; such combinations are properly evaluated under §§102 and 103, not necessarily as products of nature under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Miller and Gulack: printed matter having a functional relationship to the subject matter can render a claim patentable. The petition argues that WebOOil/WebWOil references include serving instructions that functionally relate to the oil and therefore that combination should not be treated as a product of nature. Also notes that cited oils are themselves patented (U.S. Patent 7,620,531), supporting that they are not natural products in the §101 sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: De novo review of legal determinations; broadest reasonable interpretation in examination
rubrics_metrics.description: On review, the Board's legal determinations (including claim construction and eligibility questions) are reviewed de novo; during examination pending claims receive their broadest reasonable interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Am. Acad. of Sci. Tech Ctr., 367 F.3d 1359. Petition stresses the panel failed to perform de novo review on claim construction and prior art interpretation, and improperly deferred to PTAB factual findings where legal interpretation was required. Use this standard to evaluate whether the court applied correct review scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (§102) requires clear and enabling disclosure; 'may' or equivocal language insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior-art reference must necessarily disclose and enable the claimed elements (e.g., specific dosage, ratios, steady delivery); equivocal statements ('may') or non-enabling examples do not establish anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petition contends Mark and other references use permissive language and do not enable claimed dosages/steady delivery; PHOSITA testimony on record says Mark does not enable dosage. The petition argues that the Board improperly treated such references as anticipatory despite lack of necessary enabling disclosure. Use this when evaluating whether prior art truly teaches claimed ranges and functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification and prosecution history may make claim terms limiting
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification repeatedly emphasizes certain elements (e.g., dosage tables, examples) or prosecution statements/PHOSITA testimony construe terms in a limiting way, those claim elements should be treated as limiting and cannot be excised in eligibility or anticipation analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellant points to specification tables and ~20 examples (Appx82–97) specifying dosages by age/gender and prosecution record where inventor/PHOSITA defined 'dosage' and 'casings providing controlled delivery.' The petition criticizes the Board for claiming these elements are non-limiting despite the specification and prosecution history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate §101 vs §102/§103 analyses (Mayo principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The §101 inquiry (patent-eligible subject matter) is distinct from, and should not be conflated with, novelty/obviousness (§102/§103) analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petition invokes Mayo to argue that the panel improperly applied §102-style analysis to §101 questions (e.g., looking to anticipation to decide eligibility). Courts should analyze eligibility independently from novelty/obviousness; conflation is reversible error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to address an argument is tantamount to concession
rubrics_metrics.description: A court's failure to answer an argument raised by a party may be treated as a de facto concession on that issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Herrmann and Soni: 'failure to answer an argument is tantamount to conceding there is no answer.' Petition asserts panel’s omission of responses to many of Appellant’s points equates to abandonment of those issues and warrants rehearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedents; avoid creating conflicting new law
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel opinions must conform to SCOTUS and Federal Circuit precedents (Myriad, Chakrabarty, Mayo, Alice, Rapid, etc.); opinions that attempt to alter existing rules of law or create conflicts justify en banc rehearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petition argues the panel's opinion invalidates many composition patents and conflicts with binding precedent; seeks rehearing en banc or to make opinion precedential to address conflicts per Court Operating Procedure #10(3)-(4). Emphasize checking precedential consistency when novel holdings are announced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation by composition: showing prior-art compositions contain the claimed components/ratios suffices when enabling
rubrics_metrics.description: If a prior-art composition (e.g., nutrient analyses or patent disclosing oils) expressly contains the components and ratios recited in the claim and is enabling for the claimed use/dosage, that can support anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board relied on Mark, Olive Nutrient Analysis, and Walnut Nutrient Analysis to find claims anticipated because they purportedly disclose omega-6/omega-3 ratios and serving sizes within claimed dosage limits. Petition disputes the enablement and operability of those disclosures and points to PHOSITA testimony to the contrary. Distinguish factual enablement and legal sufficiency when applying this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casing/dosage not patentable if specification treats them as non-limiting
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification expressly states a term (e.g., 'any orally accepted form') is within the scope and does not describe novel characteristics of those components, courts may find such terms do not impart patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board found 'casing' and 'dosage' not limiting because specification indicated any orally accepted form and did not describe novel characteristics. The petition disputes this characterization, citing specific tables/examples and prosecution statements, so practitioners should check specification language and prosecution history to determine whether elements are limiting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete claim review required — panel must review all relevant dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A court/panel should review all dependent and independent claims implicated by issues (e.g., §101 or §102), and omission to review particular claims may constitute procedural error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petition asserts the panel failed to review many dependent claims under §101 (§28 supra and UBBr53, 58-59) and omitted adjudication of certain independent claims (65, 91, 129, 130). When preparing or responding to appeals, ensure the court addresses each claim or provide reasons why particular claims need not be separately analyzed.
